narrative: During the 1940s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture were deeply rooted in tradition and identity. The afro, a hairstyle created by combing out natural growth of kinky hair, was likely worn by some individuals with naturally curly or straight hair, showcasing their unique textures. Cornrows, a style of three-strand braids close to the scalp, were considered traditional in many African cultures and may have been adopted by women in the diaspora. While there is limited documentation on hairstyles during this era, it is likely that protective styles such as box braids or Bantu knots were worn to minimize hair manipulation and environmental damage. Dreadlocks, a hairstyle made of rope-like strands of hair, may not have been widely practiced at this time, but could have been an emerging trend among some communities. Unfortunately, the source material does not provide sufficient information on hairstyles during the 1940s, leaving us with a glimpse into the possible diversity and richness of Black and African women's hair culture during this period.
